title: Dog
text: Dogs have multiple blood group antigens. DEA 1 is a key blood group in canine transfusion medicine, alongside other antigen systems. Blood typing and compatibility testing support donor selection. Oxyglobin provides a dog-specific historical precedent: 885 manufacturer-collected veterinary reports from 1998-1999 and 146 printed case vignettes. This descriptive archive is separate from the controlled FDA trial and does not establish BHOC efficacy or use in other species.

title: Cat
text: The feline AB blood group system includes types A, B and AB. Cats also have other red cell antigens, so AB typing alone does not establish complete transfusion compatibility. Shared hemoglobin chemistry coexists with species-specific compatibility and clinical requirements.

title: Camel
text: Camels illustrate how mammals adapt to demanding environments while retaining the core hemoglobin-based mechanism of oxygen transport. Comparative biology helps us ask better research questions. Shared physiology does not establish common dosing, safety or treatment efficacy.

title: Orangutan
text: Orangutans are Critically Endangered. Protecting these great apes connects habitat conservation, animal health and the future of forest ecosystems. The BHOC initiative brings species protection into the conversation about future animal health research. This is a conservation focus, not a therapeutic approval claim.

title: Giant Panda
text: The giant panda represents the connection between animal health, habitat protection and the future of biodiversity. Different species share a biological need for oxygen. Their physiology and conservation needs guide our research questions.

title: Marine Turtle
text: Marine turtles face species-specific conservation threats. The hawksbill turtle is classified globally as Critically Endangered by the IUCN Red List. Marine turtle imagery represents a broader biodiversity mission. Conservation status varies by species and population.

title: Horse
text: Horses have distinct red cell blood groups and transfusion requirements. The underlying hemoglobin-based transport of oxygen is shared with other mammals. Comparative physiology provides a research foundation; each veterinary application still needs its own evidence.

title: Elephant
text: Elephants bring together extraordinary mammalian biology and complex animal health and conservation needs. The initiative explores the connection between future veterinary science and species protection, without implying an approved treatment for elephants.

title: Lion
text: Lions illustrate the connection between wildlife health, functioning habitats and the wider web of biodiversity. A shared biological need for oxygen inspires comparative research. It does not remove the need for species-specific safety and efficacy studies.

The neglected cubs were taken to Noah's Ark Animal Sanctuary in Locust Grove, Georgia, United States.","They became known as BLT: Bear, Lion, Tiger. They grew up in the same habitat, playing, resting and seeking affection from one another. Their bond continued into adulthood.","Baloo needed surgery to remove a harness that had grown into his skin. Sanctuary curator Allison Hedgecoth told ABC that Leo and Shere Khan became agitated while he was away. After the operation, Baloo returned to his companions.","Leo died in 2016 and Shere Khan in 2018. Baloo, the last surviving member of the trio, died on 6 May 2025 after veterinarians made the decision to euthanize him following declining health. The three had shared around 15 years together. text: {"slug":"hachiko","section":"Stories That Matter","title":"Hachikō: Loyalty, Dignity and Respect","description":"A values story about Hachikō, extraordinary loyalty, and the people who learned to recognize and respect it.","canonical":"https://bhocvet.com/initiative/hachiko.html","datePublished":"2026-09-23","dateModified":"2026-09-23","deck":"This is not simply the story of a dog waiting at a railway station. It is a story of loyalty, patience, acceptance, steadfastness and memory. It is also a story about people who learned to recognize and respect a remarkable life.","images":[{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4a/Hachiko_on_watch.webp","alt":"Hachikō waiting at Shibuya Station around 1933","width":800,"height":567,"caption":"Hachikō waiting at Shibuya Station, circa 1933.","credit":"Unknown photographer","license":"Public domain","href":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hachiko_on_watch.webp"},{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/Death_of_Hachiko_-_Last_Photo.jpg","alt":"People paying respect to Hachikō at Shibuya Station on 8 March 1935","width":700,"height":544,"caption":"People paying respect to Hachikō at Shibuya Station on 8 March 1935.","credit":"Shibuya Folk and Literary Shirane Memorial Museum / Yamato Shimbun","license":"Public domain","href":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Death_of_Hachiko_-_Last_Photo.jpg"}],"values":["Loyalty","Patience","Acceptance","Steadfastness","Memory","Respect"],"paragraphs":["After Professor Hidesaburō Ueno died in 1925, Hachikō continued returning to Shibuya Station, where he had once met him after work.","He kept returning for years. His constancy became a symbol of loyalty, but the story is also about something else: the ability of people to recognize meaning in the life of another species.","Hachikō could not explain his attachment in human language. People had to observe, understand and accept it on its own terms.","Eventually they did. He became known and cared for around the station, and in 1934 a bronze statue honoring him was unveiled while he was still alive.","That combination is what makes the story exceptional: extraordinary loyalty from one living being, and respect from others who learned to see it."],"principle":"Respect does not begin when another living being can speak our language. It begins when we are willing to understand theirs.","closing":"A remarkable animal. A great soul. Its position builds on a longer tradition of Catholic environmental teaching rather than establishing a new universal legal rule."]},{"heading":"Why this matters for animal welfare and veterinary medicine","paragraphs":["The message invites a practical question: how can responsibility for the natural world translate into better protection for habitats, species and individual animals?","Wildlife veterinarians, conservation researchers and animal welfare teams work where these concerns intersect. text: {"slug":"veterinary-oncology-hypoxia","navLabel":"Veterinary oncology: hypoxia and oxygen-delivery questions","navActive":"science.html","breadcrumbs":[{"label":"Research topics","href":"topics.html"}],"title":"Veterinary Tumor Hypoxia and Oxygen Research | BHOC Vet","description":"Explore how preclinical tumor-oxygenation findings could inform veterinary research, with clear separation of rat, mouse, canine, feline and equine evidence.","schemaType":"WebPage","datePublished":"2026-10-25","dateModified":"2026-10-25","eyebrow":"Veterinary evidence and research","heading":"Veterinary oncology: hypoxia and oxygen-delivery questions","lead":"Veterinary oncology needs species- and tumor-specific evidence. This research overview asks how existing oxygen-transport and tumor-oxygenation studies could inform a carefully defined veterinary programme.","topicSections":[{"id":"models","title":"Identify the model before interpreting the finding","paragraphs":["The library includes rat HBOC-201 tumor studies and mouse work on polymerized human hemoglobin. These records offer preclinical context. They are not clinical tumor-treatment trials in dogs, cats or horses, and they do not establish BHOC efficacy.","One retained rat study reported no effect on fractionated-irradiation response. Such results belong beside oxygenation measurements when a potential combination with radiotherapy is considered. An oxygen signal alone is not a tumor-response endpoint."],"links":[{"label":"Rat irradiation result: PMID 16254709","href":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16254709/","detail":"Negative treatment-response finding retained in the evidence."},{"label":"Mouse oxygen-affinity and tumor-oxygenation study","href":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32647211/","detail":"Polymerized human hemoglobin in a mouse model."},{"label":"Broader tumor-hypoxia evidence route","href":"https://bhoctherapeutics.com/applications/oncology-tumor-oxygenation/","detail":""}],"bullets":[]},{"id":"species","title":"Dogs, cats and horses need separate study questions","paragraphs":["A canine or feline oncology proposal should name the tumor type, treatment context, starting oxygenation and measurable outcome. An equine question requires its own rationale and source base. The biological theme does not remove differences in disease, physiology or clinical practice.","The historical Oxyglobin material on canine anemia and feline case experience should remain identifiable as such. It does not become evidence of anticancer activity merely because an anemic animal also has cancer."],"links":[{"label":"Oxyglobin and canine anemia evidence","href":"./oxyglobin.html#canine-anemia","detail":""},{"label":"Feline anemia and historical oxygen-carrier evidence","href":"./feline-blood-transfusion-compatibility.html#feline-anemia","detail":""},{"label":"Equine physiological research","href":"./science.html#equine-oxygenation","detail":""}],"bullets":[]},{"id":"transport","title":"Transport models answer a narrower question","paragraphs":["The hepatic hollow-fiber bioreactor paper indexed as PMID 19816963 is a mathematical oxygen-transport model involving hemoglobin-based carriers and perfluorocarbons. It is not a veterinary tumor-treatment experiment.","It can help define a transport question, while animal tumor studies, clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy remain separate steps. The human research overview explains this distinction and the separate oxygen-sensing foundations."],"links":[{"label":"Transport-model scope and HIF/VHL context","href":"https://bhoctherapeutics.com/applications/oncology-tumor-oxygenation/#transport-model","detail":""}],"bullets":[]},{"id":"programme","title":"A proposed BHOC veterinary oncology programme","paragraphs":["We propose beginning with a defined experimental or veterinary setting and measuring oxygen availability over time. A study would need a characterized formulation, an appropriate comparison, safety measurements and a prespecified tissue or treatment-response endpoint.","Our hypothesis concerns controlled tissue oxygen delivery, including its duration and consistency. Whether it changes tumor biology or treatment response is a question to test. The current sources do not establish a BHOC cancer treatment."],"links":[{"label":"Research questions on oxygen exposure and tissue response","href":"https://bhoctherapeutics.com/evidence/library/concepts-hypotheses/oxygen-exposure-transport-delivery-tissue-response.html","detail":""},{"label":"BHOC joint-research invitation","href":"./bhoc-crada-research-partners.html","detail":""}],"bullets":["Identify the species, tumor type and model rather than pooling them.","Separate anemia support from the proposed tumor-directed endpoint.","Measure the oxygen time course and the relevant biological response.","Retain negative results and product-specific limitations in the final interpretation."]}],"topicCards":[]}

title: From nature. Through science. Back to nature.
text: ×  BHOC Veterinary. BHOC Vet.  From nature. Through science. Back to nature.  BHOC Veterinary Therapeutics, also known as BHOC Vet, is led by Archil Jaliashvili. The BHOC Species & Biodiversity Protection Initiative connects oxygen delivery science with the future of animal health and species protection.  Our foundation is comparative biology: different species have different blood group systems, yet most vertebrates share hemoglobin-based oxygen transport. We explore how this foundation can inform species-specific research and development.  Meet BHOC Therapeutics
